info.bio: Killing Joke se creo  en 1979, cuando “Big Paul” Ferguson (batería original) conoció a Jaz Coleman en Notting Hill, en el área de Londres. A ellos se unieron Geordie Walker y Martin ‘Youth’ Glover como bajista. De acuerdo con Coleman, su propósito era “definir la exquisita belleza de la era atómica en términos de estilo, sonido y forma”. Crearon su propio sello, Malicious Damage (que consiguió acuerdo de distribución con Island y después pasó a EG Records).

scenes.name: Postpunk sombrío de segunda generación
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Toda edad de oro fabrica su propio final: tras PiL y Joy Division surge un underground de bandas lúgubres (The Sound, Killing Joke) y la segunda edición del festival Futurama (1980) parece un Monsters of Rock angustiado, rebaños de muchachos en sobretodo gris tan uniformes como los fans de Iron Maiden. El pico de 1979 —Fear of Music, Metal Box, Unknown Pleasures, Setting Sons, Entertainment! en la lista de NME— es también el principio del declive.

scenes.name: Gótico
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Término que Hannett aplicó a Joy Division y luego insulto para los epígonos, hasta que en 1982 los fans lo adoptan como estandarte frente a la excesiva luminosidad del new pop: glamour sepulcral, retorno de lo reprimido, emociones atemporales. Bauhaus («Bela Lugosi's Dead», 1979, el comienzo propiamente dicho; Peter Murphy, sex symbol heredero de Adam Ant y Bowie), The Birthday Party (el gótico americano de Nick Cave: «Release the Bats», Junkyard), Killing Joke («música de tensión», del funk de PiL a Black Sabbath, con un aura inquietante), The Cure (gótico light: Seventeen Seconds, Faith, Pornography). El club The Batcave (1982), el «positive punk», Southern Death Cult, Theatre of Hate, The Sisters of Mercy («¡Nosotros sí somos una banda de rock!»), el death rock de Los Ángeles y Kukl con Björk. Su deriva: coqueteos totalitarios y la conversión en versión postpunk del heavy metal (The Cult).

scenes.name: Dark punk y rock gótico
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El punk británico estuvo flanqueado desde el principio por un movimiento «gótico» que canalizaba su violencia hacia atmósferas de terror y rituales esotéricos: Stranglers, Siouxsie, X-Ray Spex. Lo más interesante evita el tono de película de terror: The Cure introducen la angustia existencial de Camus y Sartre (Pornography, Disintegration); Joy Division mezclan Doors, Kraftwerk y Black Sabbath y su final anuncia el synth-pop; Bauhaus, Killing Joke, Psychedelic Furs, los irlandeses Virgin Prunes y la cima del género, Public Image Ltd de Johnny Lydon, que convierte el punk en música de cámara con dub y ecos étnicos (Second Edition, Flowers Of Romance). Después, el gótico bailable de Sisters Of Mercy, Alien Sex Fiend, Cult, Mission e In The Nursery.

podcast.title: Disappearance to Iceland (1982)
podcast.body: Following a gig in Brighton, England, Jaz Coleman suddenly disappeared. He made two phone calls, one to his mother to assure her he was alright and another to Killing Joke's record label. He then traveled to Iceland, believing it to be the safest place on the planet based on his interpretations. "So after a gig in Brighton England he suddenly disappeared."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Jaz Coleman's Apocalyptic Beliefs (1982)
podcast.body: After the release of the album "Revelations" in 1982, singer Jaz Coleman became convinced that the world was truly about to end. He determined this through various occult means, coincidentally sharing a birthday with cult master Alistair Crowley. "After the album hit the stores, singer jazz Coleman decided that the world really was about to end."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Jazz Coleman Quits for Apocalypse (1982)
podcast.body: In February 1982, following a performance, singer Jazz Coleman announced his departure from Killing Joke and his intention to move to Iceland. He was convinced that the apocalypse was near and believed Iceland offered the safest refuge. This conviction stemmed from his deep fascination with the occult and a growing paranoia developed after investigating various conspiracy theories concerning the end of the world. Shortly after, guitarist Jordy Walker joined him in Iceland, seemingly persuaded by Coleman's apocalyptic reasoning. "After a gig, he announced he was quitting killing joke and moving to Iceland."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Seven Months Awaiting Apocalypse (1982)
podcast.body: Jaz Coleman and Geordie spent seven months in Iceland, waiting for the apocalypse that never materialized. During this time, they worked with various Icelandic bands, one of which eventually evolved into The Sugarcubes, featuring Björk. After seven months, they gave up and returned to England. "For seven months of wedding for the apocalypse they gave up and went back to England."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Severing Ties and Geordie's Support (April 7, 1982)
podcast.body: On April 7, 1982, Jaz Coleman released a statement formally severing all his remaining ties with Killing Joke. However, Geordie, the band's guitarist, believed Coleman's apocalyptic theories and flew to Iceland to join him. "On April 7th 1982, Jazz released a statement severing all his remaining ties with Killing Joke."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Jazz Coleman's Disappearance (2012)
podcast.body: In July 2012, Jazz Coleman unexpectedly disappeared. He appeared to be upset about Killing Joke's impending tour with The Cult and expressed a strong desire to dissociate himself from both the tour and the band, which was publicly voiced in a scathing Facebook post. Approximately a month later, he was located living a "nomadic existence" in the Western Sahara. Coleman subsequently claimed that the controversial Facebook post was not authored by him but by an imposter. "Jazz seemed angry that killing joke was going on tour with the cult, and he didn't want to have anything to do with the road trip or the band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 12-inch Remix Business
podcast.body: Killing Joke participated in the 12-inch remix trend, a popular format in the 1980s for bands seeking to expand their presence in dance clubs, following the lead of New Order's "Blue Monday." "And so was Depeche Mode and The Cure and The Human League and Simple Minds and The Cult and Killing Joke and Erasure and Psychedelic Furs and Madness. They all got into the 12-inch business."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Band Formation and Influence
podcast.body: Killing Joke is described as a heavy post-punk group originating from England, which began releasing records in 1980. The band has been a significant influence on a diverse range of artists, including Tool, Nine Inch Nails, Metallica, Nirvana, the Foo Fighters, Jane's Addiction, Marilyn Manson, and Soundgarden. Additionally, Jimmy Page of Led Zeppelin is noted as a massive admirer of their work. "Killing joke has been a big influence on tool, 9-inch nails, Metallica, both Nirvana and the Food Fighters, Jane's Addiction, Marilyn Manson and Soundgarden."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Collaboration with Dave Grohl
podcast.body: Despite the past controversy surrounding "Come As You Are," all appears to be forgiven between the bands, as Dave Grohl (formerly of Nirvana) has since performed and recorded with Killing Joke. "Kurt is gone and Dave Grohl has performed and recorded with killing joke."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Formation of Niceland
podcast.body: During their time in Iceland, following Jazz Coleman's departure from Killing Joke due to his apocalyptic beliefs, he and Jordy Walker engaged with the local rock scene, assisting various musicians. It was during this period that they formed a new band, which they named Niceland, before eventually returning to England. "after spending time helping various people within the Icelandic rock scene and forming a band they called Niceland, jazz and Jordy returned to England."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

"quedaron fascinados con los conciertos de Killin Joke y Bout House, comenzaron a cardarse el pelo y a vestir con pantalones de piel y creepers."

podcast.title: Plagiarism Claim Against Nirvana
podcast.body: Killing Joke's song "80s" (1985), co-written by Jazz Coleman, was observed to have a guitar riff strikingly similar to Nirvana's "Come As You Are" (1991). The situation regarding a lawsuit remains unclear, with conflicting reports on whether action was taken or dropped after Kurt Cobain's death, or simply considered but not pursued for financial/personal reasons. "Some sources say that there was a lawsuit, but that it was dropped after Kurt Cobain commuted suicide. Others say that even though they considered suing, killing joke decided not to take any action on copyright infringement for personal and financial reasons."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Andy Rourke Death (May 18, 2023) – Pancreatic Cancer, Age 59; Sued Morrissey, Later Played Two Morrissey Singles
xref.body: Andy Rourke was a founding member of the Smiths and is considered by fans one of the greatest bassists in the history of British indie rock. His time with the band ended badly: a heroin addiction, a lawsuit against Morrissey and Johnny Marr for unpaid royalties (he was broke), and a decade later a bankruptcy over tax issues. Post-Smiths, he worked with the Pretenders, Killing Joke, Stone Roses singer Ian Brown, Dolores O'Riordan and the Cranberries, and Peter Hook of New Order. In a remarkable reconciliation, he played on two Morrissey solo singles despite the money disputes. His father and sister were both diagnosed with cancer, which prompted him to start a cancer charity; he himself was later diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. He died in a New York hospital on May 18, 2023, age 59. "Ask any Smiths fan, and they'll tell you that he was one of the greatest bassists in the history of British Indie Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: "Come As You Are" Plagiarism Claim (Killing Joke)
xref.body: Nirvana's "Come As You Are" (1991) shared a distinct guitar riff similarity with Killing Joke's 1985 song "80s," co-written by Jazz Coleman. The status of a potential lawsuit is unclear, with some sources claiming it was dropped after Kurt Cobain's suicide, and others suggesting Killing Joke opted not to sue for personal and financial reasons. Despite past issues, Dave Grohl has since performed and recorded with Killing Joke, signaling a resolution. "Some sources say that there was a lawsuit, but that it was dropped after Kurt Cobain commuted suicide. Others say that even though they considered suing, killing joke decided not to take any action on copyright infringement for personal and financial reasons."

xref.title: Broadway Musical Character
xref.body: John Bechtel is the touring keyboard player for Ministry and has also played with Fear Factory, Killing Joke, and Prong. He is a character in both the graphic novel *Funhouse* and its subsequent Broadway musical adaptation, which were created by his sister, Alice Bechtel. "John is actually a character in both, but Alice is best known for creating the Bechtel Test, which is the test that measures the representation of women in fiction."

xref.title: Co-writer of Killing Joke's "80s"
xref.body: Jazz Coleman was the singer and co-writer of Killing Joke's 1985 song "80s." He noticed the similarities between his band's song and Nirvana's "Come As You Are" but whether a lawsuit was filed or pursued remains unclear. "Jazz Coleman was the singer and co-writer of 80s. And yes, he did notice the similarities, but did he ever do anything about it? It's actually very unclear."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Controversy Threatens "Nevermind" Momentum
xref.body: The controversy surrounding "Come As You Are" and its similarity to Killing Joke's "80s" in 1992 posed a significant threat to the song's release as the second single from "Nevermind." There was concern about how a potential lawsuit preventing the single's release could have interrupted the album's overall momentum throughout 1992, potentially altering the course of 90s music. "And what might have happened to the momentum of Never Mind as a whole throughout 1992? Had that momentum been interrupted by a lawsuit? Things might have turned out really a lot different."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Killing Joke's Reaction and Dave Grohl's Friendship
xref.body: While similarities between "Come As You Are" and Killing Joke's "Eighties" were noted by Killing Joke's singer Jazz Coleman, it's unclear if legal action was taken. Some believe it was initiated and then stopped after Kurt Cobain's death in 1994, while others say Killing Joke's respect for Nirvana prevented it. Ultimately, "all is forgiven" as Dave Grohl is "great friends with killing joke" and has "performed and toured with him." "Whatever the case, all is forgiven in the Nirvana killing joke situation."
